bibl.title: The ENCODE Blacklist: Identification of Problematic Regions of the Genome

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A PUBLISHED LIST OF WHAT DOES NOT COUNT - genomic regions excluded from every ENCODE analysis by convention, and now from many pipelines outside it
span.quote: Here, we define the ENCODE blacklist- a comprehensive set of regions in the human, mouse, worm, and fly genomes that have anomalous, unstructured, or high signal in next-generation sequencing experiments independent of cell line or experiment. The removal of the ENCODE blacklist is an essential quality measure when analyzing functional genomics data.

span.label: which regions of a genome produce signal that is an artefact of the assembly rather than of the sample, and how to identify them without hand curation
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.label: an automated, threshold-based blacklist for human, mouse, worm and fly, replacing a hand-curated list - and a demonstration that applying it changes published correlations
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.label: method

span.label: regions where the reference assembly is wrong or incomplete, which collect reads at up to 6,400x background and are then read as biology
span.quote: The signal at blacklist regions are extremely high even though they account for a small fraction of the mappable chromosome (Fig. 1b ). For example, this represented 582 million of 2.5 billion uniquely aligning reads mapping to blacklisted regions in the human ENCODE ChIP-seq data in hg19.

span.label: score every 1 kb window of input ChIP-seq data across many cell types for read depth and multi-mapping rate, quantile normalise, take the median, and flag the top 1%
span.term: score every 1 kb window of input ChIP-seq data across many cell types for read depth and multi-mapping rate, quantile normalise, take the median, and flag the top 1%
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.label: THE ARTEFACT IS A PROPERTY OF THE REFERENCE, NOT OF THE SAMPLE: `the major differences between blacklists are due to underlying changes in THE SEQUENCE ASSEMBLIES ... THE DRIVING FACTOR BEHIND ARTIFACT REGIONS IN THE GENOME ARE DUE TO ISSUES IN THE ASSEMBLY RATHER THAN OTHER FACTORS`. Change the reference and the exclusion list changes
span.quote: Overall, these differences lead to the conclusion that the major differences between blacklists are due to underlying changes in the sequence assemblies. Consequently, this lends to the hypothesis that the driving factor behind artifact regions in the genome are due to issues in the assembly rather than other factors.

span.label: and the failure mode is an ILLUSION OF STRUCTURE: `blacklist regions sequester a large portion of ChIP-seq reads, LEADING TO AN ILLUSION OF HIGH CORRELATION of these regions with others. After blacklist filtering, the correlation structure is more distinct`. The artefact does not add noise, it adds AGREEMENT
span.quote: In the unfiltered set of peaks, blacklist regions sequester a large portion of ChIP-seq reads, leading to an illusion of high correlation of these regions with others. After blacklist filtering, the correlation structure is more distinct.

span.label: THE LIST REMOVES ~3% OF HUMAN PROTEIN CODING GENES FROM ANALYSIS, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: `those studying genes in unmappable regions of the genome WILL FIND THEIR DATA FILTERED BY THE BLACKLIST`. A researcher whose gene is on the list cannot study it with these pipelines
span.quote: Finally, those studying genes in unmappable regions of the genome will find their data filtered by the blacklist. These regions account for ~3% of human protein coding genes that have previously been shown to be unmappable using short-read technologies

span.label: IT IS BOUND TO ONE REFERENCE VERSION: `the blacklists are SPECIFIC TO EACH GENOME ASSEMBLY and A LIFT OVER FROM AN OLD ASSEMBLY IS NOT MEANINGFUL OR VALID`. The list is not a fact about the genome; it is a fact about a build of the genome
span.quote: We also caution that the blacklists are specific to each genome assembly and a lift over from an old assembly is not meaningful or valid.

span.label: and it is ASSAY-SPECIFIC, declared against the paper's own generality: `WE DO NOT PROPOSE A SINGLE BLACKLIST that can encapsulate error defined across all NGS based assays ... THE SAME CRITERIA CANNOT BE APPLIED for whole genome sequencing filtering and RNA-seq filtering`
span.quote: It is important to note that we do not propose a single blacklist that can encapsulate error defined across all NGS based assays. The presented blacklist shows high concordance between chromatin-based filtering (DNase/ATAC-DAC blacklist) and ChIP-seq input based filtering. This is not surprising given that the input DNA for ChIP-seq has been shown to be a proxy for lightly digested open chromatin assays 8 . However, the same criteria cannot be applied for whole genome sequencing (WGS) filtering and RNA-seq filtering.

span.label: the threshold is A CHOICE STATED AS ONE: regions in `THE TOP 1%` of read depth or multi-mapping rate `are considered LIKELY artifacts`. Nothing in the paper derives 1%; it is where the line was put
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.label: and the list it replaces MISSED AN ENTIRE CRITERION: nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments were `A CRITERION THAT WAS OVERLOOKED IN THE INITIAL MANUAL BLACKLISTS`. The hand-curated version had been in production use for years
span.quote: Almost all of the flagged regions also included nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs, Supplemental Fig. 2c ), a criterion that was overlooked in the initial manual blacklists.

span.label: the blacklist was built from INPUT samples - randomly sheared, non-immunoprecipitated chromatin - across many cell types, quantile normalised, median taken
span.note: eliminates: cell-line-specific signal (copy number variants) and processing differences as sources of the flagged regions; the paper says the multiple cell types are there for exactly that · outcome: held
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.label: whether applying the list changes conclusions, tested on a named case
span.note: eliminates: the objection that filtering is cosmetic - REST, a known repressor, auto-correlates with activating factors UNTIL the blacklist is applied, and the spurious correlation `HAS ESSENTIALLY DISAPPEARED as would be expected given the known biology` · outcome: held
span.quote: As a specific example, the correlation of REST (a known repressor) auto correlates with other TFs (most of them activating) without the filtering of the blacklist. The removal of the blacklist regions removes spurious correlations seen with REST has essentially disappeared as would be expected given the known biology.

span.label: whether the 1% threshold is derived
span.note: eliminates: nothing - regions in `the top 1%` are `considered LIKELY artifacts`, and no derivation, sensitivity analysis or alternative cut is offered · outcome: failed
span.quote: Regions with read depths or multi-mapping read rates in the top 1% are considered likely artifacts (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). In all cases, the mitochondrial DNA and any reads mapping to these sequences are pre-filtered from analysis and are considered part of the blacklist.

span.quote: Here, we define the ENCODE blacklist- a comprehensive set of regions in the human, mouse, worm, and fly genomes that have anomalous, unstructured, or high signal in next-generation sequencing experiments independent of cell line or experiment. The removal of the ENCODE blacklist is an essential quality measure when analyzing functional genomics data.

span.label: Duke Excluded Regions
span.term: Duke Excluded Regions
span.quote: The original ENCODE blacklist, termed the Duke Excluded Regions (DER), was manually curated on the Homo sapiens (human) genome assembly GRCh37 (hereafter referred to as hg19) to cover a large number of repeat elements in the genome, particularly rRNA, alpha satellites, and other simple repeats. This list was further updated, now referred to as ENCODE Data Analysis Center (DAC) blacklisted regions, to include regions of high signal that presumably represent unannotated repeats in the genome.

span.quote: The original ENCODE blacklist, termed the Duke Excluded Regions (DER), was manually curated on the Homo sapiens (human) genome assembly GRCh37 (hereafter referred to as hg19) to cover a large number of repeat elements in the genome, particularly rRNA, alpha satellites, and other simple repeats. span.label: what changed about the field: these regions `HAVE GENERALLY BEEN IGNORED AND UNFILTERED BECAUSE THEY HAVE NOT BEEN FOUND TO AFFECT the signal in the final analyses` - and the paper's case is that in ChIP-seq they `CAN DRAMATICALLY BIAS THE RESULTS`. The same regions, a different assay, an opposite verdict
span.quote: Problematic regions such as these have generally been ignored and unfiltered because they have not been found to affect the signal in the final analyses. However, in functional genomics assays such as chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by genome sequencing (ChIP-seq), accuracy in peak calling and downstream analyses is essential. Alignments in these problematic regions should be identified and filtered before application of any threshold, normalization, or peak calling as they can dramatically bias the results
